label: Title
notes: Open by framing the Voronoi diagram as a nearest-neighbor data structure drawn directly in the plane. Explain that the lecture will keep translating the same object into more inspectable certificates: inequalities for individual cells, adjacency for Delaunay edges, empty circles for vertices, and lower hull facets after lifting. The title diagram should be read as a map of winning regions, not as decoration.

label: Lecture Map
notes: Use this roadmap as the contract for the hour. Each tile is a different computational handle on the same nearest-site geometry, so students should expect the representations to reinforce one another rather than feel like a list of unrelated facts. Pause on the word translation: the course theme is turning continuous geometric definitions into finite objects an algorithm can update and verify.

label: Nearest-Site Rule
notes: Emphasize the inclusive inequality in the definition. Boundaries are not gaps between cells; they are exactly the places where at least two nearest-site certificates are simultaneously true. After naming the sites, ask students what happens to a query point as it crosses a black edge in the diagram. The answer should be that the winning site changes while distances to the two adjacent sites tie on the edge.

label: Bisectors
notes: Walk through the cancellation rather than expanding every coordinate in full. The key move is that comparing squared distances removes the x dot x term and leaves a first-degree inequality in the query point. This is the first major simplification of the chapter: a nonlinear-sounding proximity condition becomes a half-plane bounded by a perpendicular bisector.

label: Half-Plane Cell
notes: This is the computational heart of a single Voronoi cell. The final polygon is not guessed from a picture; it is the feasible region of several simple linear inequalities, one for each competing site. Point out that each side of the blue polygon has an owner, meaning a specific competing site whose bisector became tight along that boundary segment.

label: Bounded Cells
notes: Connect unbounded cells to supporting lines of the site set. For a hull site, there is an outward direction in which every other site stays behind a supporting line, so the hull site keeps winning arbitrarily far away. For an interior site, competing sites surround it, and the half-plane intersection closes up into a bounded polygon.

label: Duality
notes: Ask students to track one black Voronoi edge and then locate the red segment joining the two sites on either side of it. That pairing is the operational meaning of the dual. The red Delaunay edge is not the same geometric object as the black Voronoi edge; it records which two regions touch and usually crosses the corresponding Voronoi edge at right angles.

label: Empty Circle
notes: The empty circle is the shortest bridge from Voronoi vertices to Delaunay triangles. The center is not arbitrary: it is the point where three nearest-site inequalities become equalities. Stress the word empty as a certificate. If a fourth site were inside the circle, then the center would be closer to that fourth site and could not be a Voronoi vertex for the displayed triple.

label: Complexity
notes: The important surprise is linearity, not the exact constants alone. Pairwise bisectors form a quadratic family, but the planar subdivision cannot keep all of their pieces visible. Explain the auxiliary vertex at infinity as a counting device for unbounded rays, then connect Euler counting and degree constraints to the bounds on vertices and edges.

label: Insertion
notes: Present insertion through the Delaunay dual because the changing region is easy to certify. The marked triangles are precisely those whose empty-circle promise is broken by the new site. Once those triangles are removed, the boundary of the cavity is the stable part of the old triangulation, and connecting the new site to that boundary produces the updated local star.

label: Locality And Worst Case
notes: Use this slide to keep the algorithmic story honest. The update is local in the sense that only the cavity changes, but the cavity itself can be large under an adversarial insertion order. This distinction matters for algorithm analysis: a clean geometric certificate explains what must be changed, while randomized ordering or additional data structures control the expected amount of work.

label: Paraboloid Lifting
notes: The purpose of lifting is conceptual compression. Empty-circle tests in the plane become lower-supporting-plane tests in three dimensions, so a proximity statement is turned into a convex hull statement. Point to the lifted points first, then to the projected lower hull chain, and make clear that the red planar triangulation is a shadow of lower hull incidence.

label: Voronoi As Shadow
notes: Treat this as a synthesis slide. Delaunay and Voronoi are not two unrelated diagrams placed on top of the same sites; they are two projections of one incidence structure. Delaunay focuses on which sites share empty circles, while Voronoi focuses on where the centers of those empty circles live and how adjacent centers connect.

label: Point-Line Duality
notes: Use point-line duality as the chapter closing move from proximity diagrams to a broader computational geometry principle. Incidence is preserved, vertical order is reversed, and lower envelopes become upper hull chains. The exact formula is less important than the habit it teaches: transform the problem until a reliable primitive, such as convex hull, becomes the natural engine.

label: Moving A Site
notes: Tie the applied lab back to certificates. Continuous motion changes the coordinates of boundaries continuously, but the combinatorial structure changes only at discrete events such as a tie crossing or a cocircular configuration. Ask students what measurements would reveal the event: nearest-site labels change on a raster sample, and Delaunay edges change by symmetric difference.

label: Misconceptions
notes: Use this as an interactive pause before the summary. The square example is deliberately degenerate and checks three distinctions at once: a bisector need not survive, a Voronoi edge is not a Delaunay edge, and a cocircular set may admit more than one valid triangulation. Let students predict first, then use the slide to name the convention problem.

label: Summary
notes: Close by naming the durable pattern from the chapter. Computational geometry often succeeds by changing representation until the same facts become easier to certify. Voronoi cells, Delaunay edges, empty circles, lower hull facets, and dual line envelopes are not separate tricks; they are a toolkit for converting geometric proximity and intersection questions into finite, checkable structures.
